comparator.name: Human Geography and Planning
comparator.sourceNotes: The degree includes 60 EC of first-year courses, a 30 EC track, 15 EC of major electives, 45 EC of profiling electives, and 30 EC of final-year research courses and thesis work.
components: Foundations of Human Geography and Planning
Participate in Cities in Transition and Competing Claims on Space, and pass at least one of them before taking this course.
Theories and Approaches to Migration and Global Development

Start the track after earning at least 45 EC, passing Globalization and Development and participating in Spatial Data and Geographic Information and Socio-Spatial Research. Take the four track courses in one academic year.
Global Migration and Development: Key Themes
Participate in the track theory course before taking this course.
Participate in the track themes course and pass Spatial Data and Geographic Information before starting the project.
Participate in both the theory and themes courses and pass at least one of them before starting the lab.
Choose 45 EC of electives, with at least 15 EC at intermediate level or above. Options include an eligible minor, study abroad or a placement.
Pass the Mixed Methods Research Project before taking Analysis.
Pass the eight first-year courses and complete the track before taking Research Design.
Pass the eight first-year courses, all four track courses and Research Design, and participate in Science and Society and Analysis before starting the thesis.

routeSelection.basis: This example takes Migration and Global Development, the first track in the student guide. The electives use different timetable slots from the required track courses.

alternatives.label: Cities, Communities and Spatial Sustainability
alternatives.concept: Study how people and institutions shape places and respond to environmental change. Combine social research and economics with geographic data, Earth observation, delta management and applied spatial planning.
alternatives.labelReason: The title reflects the main question and selected course contributions.
progression: Sustainability foundations and introductory data science precede Earth Observation and Spatial Planning. Introductory research methods precede Econometrics.

alternatives.label: Migration, Global Development and Place
alternatives.concept: Study how empire, conflict, economic change and migration connect places across borders. Explore how these forces shape communities and identities through political analysis, cultural history and social research.
alternatives.labelReason: The title reflects the main question and selected course contributions.
alternatives.distinctness: This plan differs by 13 courses from the broad plan and by 8 courses from the other focused plan, in each direction.
progression: History of Empires and the politics foundations precede more focused work on colonial histories, public policy and conflict. Qualitative methods precede the advanced historical research seminar.

alternatives.label: Urban Governance, Inequality and Policy
alternatives.concept: Study how public decisions shape access to housing, services and a healthy environment. Connect social inequality and community action with public economics, rights, comparative institutions and policy communication.
alternatives.labelReason: The title reflects the main question and selected course contributions.
alternatives.distinctness: This plan differs by 10 courses from the broad plan and by 8 courses from the other focused plan, in each direction.
progression: Introduction to Economics and research methods precede Public Economics. Law, Society & Justice precedes comparative constitutional law and private law.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Human geography and spatial planning across local, national and global scales
Urban change, housing, mobility, inequality and inclusive public space
Spatial, quantitative, qualitative and mixed-method research using geographic data and field evidence
Planning, governance and practical intervention in contested uses of space
Independent place-based research culminating in a bachelor thesis
adjacent: Migration, global development, mobility and transnational places
Inclusive cities, wellbeing, equality and access
Climate adaptation, sustainable cities, regions and environmental transitions
questions: How can cities and regions become more sustainable, inclusive and resilient?
How do global trends, migration and political-economic change reshape local places?
How can spatial data, field research and stakeholder evidence support defensible planning decisions?

candidates.label: Migration, Global Development and Place
candidates.assessment: Conflict and forced migration, international political economy, histories of empire and regional mobility, policy and human rights are coherent foundations for studying migration and place. Specialist migration geography and field placement remain distinct.

candidates.label: Urban Governance, Inequality and Policy
candidates.assessment: The plan studies access and inequality through sociology, public economics, comparative institutions, property law and community action. It leaves specialized housing, transit and urban-design training to further study.

candidates.label: Planning sustainable cities
candidates.reason: The direction is coherent and evidenced, but three UCR alternatives are already included.

candidates.label: Innovative and sustainable regions
candidates.reason: The direction is coherent and evidenced, but three UCR alternatives are already included.

trace: Develops reflective collaboration and professional practice for multidisciplinary place-based work.
Provides economic concepts for land, housing, regional development and urban change.
Explains international economic linkages and shocks that connect regional and global development.
analyzes public goods, externalities, redistribution and the equity and efficiency of public services
Provides regression-based quantitative analysis for relationships among economic, social and spatial outcomes.
develops measurement, sampling, surveys and statistical inference for empirical social research
studies stress, identity safety and inclusive leadership in organizations as a supporting perspective on inclusion
Introduces computational data handling and visualisation for evidence about places and populations.
Examines how communities and institutions live with water in vulnerable landscapes.
Studies circular recovery and remediation as material interventions in regional environments.
Analyses institutions, stakeholders and policy choices in environmental governance.
Uses remote sensing and geospatial evidence to observe land and environmental change.
Develops quantitative tools for analysing coupled earth systems and environmental patterns.
Introduces linked environmental, social and economic dimensions of sustainability in places.
applies chemistry, materials, waves and experimental measurement to sustainability investigations
Explains climate processes, impacts and adaptation questions central to spatial futures.
uses GIS, remote sensing and practical projects for environmental monitoring, disaster response and sustainable land use
Introduces legal, social and normative analysis of institutions governing everyday life.
Historicises empire and the uneven global relations that have shaped regions and mobility.
studies Indigenous communities and land through histories of colonization, dispossession and cultural resilience
Requires independent source-based research, argumentation and academic writing in an advanced seminar.
Examines rights and justice claims relevant to exclusion, inequality and inclusive cities.
Provides the international legal frame through which states, borders and transnational issues operate.
Compares constitutional and administrative structures through which public interventions are authorised.
uses comparative private law to examine ownership, possession and restrictions on property use, relevant to land governance
Builds comparative analysis of political institutions and their effects on public decisions.
Explains globalisation, geopolitics and relations that connect places across borders.
Examines multilevel European governance that materially shapes regions and cities.
uses a globalization case to analyze policy development across national and international arenas and write policy memos
Analyses conflict, peacebuilding and displacement-related political dynamics across places.
Introduces the concepts and scales needed to analyse people, institutions and societies in place.
Develops interviewing, ethnographic observation, coding and reflexive qualitative inquiry.
Provides modern sociological theories for interpreting inequality, identity and social change.
Connects collective action, environmental justice and unequal exposure to spatial-environmental harms.
Engages advanced contemporary debates about power, institutions and changing societies.
Explains how social settings and groups shape behaviour, identity and relations among residents.
Examines political psychology, youth, identity and resilience in transnational conflict contexts.
Analyses how climate claims and urban-environmental futures are publicly framed and contested.
Develops evidence-based persuasion for communicating policy and planning proposals.
Examines African art and heritage as expressions of place, identity and contested cultural ownership.
Connects Mediterranean places through mobility, exchange and cross-regional cultural history.
Examines how racial power, privilege and resistance are represented in public culture.
blocks: Both use delta environments to study water management, environmental risk and adaptation.
Utrecht studies how planning decisions mediate competing claims on land.
Both use geographic data and maps to investigate spatial change. UCR emphasizes GIS and Earth observation.
Utrecht examines planning theories. UCR applies spatial tools to environmental problems.
Utrecht studies how places are represented in media. UCR examines race, power and representation in media.
Utrecht studies urban change through human geography and planning. UCR introduces broader social structures and inequality.
Governance, policy, law and political economy
Utrecht introduces the intellectual foundations of geography and planning.
Utrecht develops theories linking migration and development across regions. UCR studies broader theories of international relations.
Utrecht studies uneven development and connections between places. UCR examines global relationships through the history of empire.
Utrecht examines debates about migration, mobility and regional development.
Utrecht applies migration research in a specialist practice lab.
Utrecht combines study of European borders with geographical fieldwork.
Spatial, quantitative, qualitative and research methods
Utrecht develops analysis for geographical research. UCR teaches econometric methods.
Both develop empirical research design, measurement and data analysis. Utrecht applies these methods to socio-spatial questions.
Utrecht integrates methods in a project within the migration track. UCR develops qualitative research and quantitative analysis in separate courses.
Utrecht prepares students to design a geography or planning thesis.
Utrecht connects geographical research with its role in society.
Utrecht requires a 15 EC empirical thesis. The UCR comparison shows optional independent research separately.
Choose 45 EC of electives, with at least 15 EC at intermediate level or above. Options include an eligible minor, study abroad or a placement.

selection.assessment: The closest programme integrates the target’s social-spatial, environmental and mixed-method core. The first two evidenced track directions after that core—migration/global development and inclusive cities—produce feasible, materially different UCR curricula. Planning sustainable cities and innovative sustainable regions are also coherent but production stops at the three-alternative maximum.

notes.text: Utrecht requires a sequence in human geography and planning, including a themed field or practice project and an empirical thesis. The UCR options draw on social science, environmental methods and policy to study related questions.

audience.programmeDescription: Study how people, institutions and environmental change shape cities and regions. Utrecht teaches mainly in Dutch, with some courses in English.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The Utrecht example follows the Migration and Global Development track. The UCR options emphasize spatial sustainability, migration and global development, or urban governance.
